meta.description: Karachi University past-paper MCQ bank — mechanics, energy & momentum, rotation, atomic structure, fluids, heat & waves, electricity & magnetism. Source: DIETS of DICC compilation by Syed Mohsin Jamal.
meta.footer: 🎓 Total: 120 MCQs | Source: Karachi University Past Papers (Physics)

questions.question: Q1. A book is at rest on top of a table. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: A) There is no force acting on the book.
B) The book has no inertia.
C) There is no force acting on the table.
D) The book is in equilibrium.
E) The inertia of the book is equal to the inertia of the table.

questions.explanation: A book at rest has zero net force acting on it since gravity and the table's normal force balance out — this is the definition of equilibrium.

questions.question: Q2. The property of a moving object to continue moving is what Galileo called
questions.explanation: Galileo called this tendency of a moving object to keep moving (and a resting object to stay at rest) inertia, which Newton later formalized as his First Law.

questions.question: Q3. According to Newton's First Law of Motion,

options.text: A) an object in motion eventually comes to a halt.
B) an object at rest eventually begins to move
C) an object in motion moves in a parabolic trajectory unless acted upon by a net force.
D) an object at rest always remains at rest.
E) an object at rest remains at rest unless acted upon by a net force.

questions.explanation: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia) states an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force.

questions.question: Q4. If an object is moving, then the magnitude of it's cannot be zero.
questions.explanation: Speed and velocity are magnitudes of motion, so if the object is moving they can't be zero. Acceleration, however, can be zero even while moving (e.g. constant velocity).

questions.question: Q5. A car initially at rest accelerates in a straight line at 3 m/s². What will be its speed after 2 seconds?
Q6. A body in free fall in a vacuum

options.text: A) will drop the same distance during each second of its fall.
B) will have the same average speed during each second of its fall.
C) will have a constant velocity during each second of its fall.
D) Will not be accelerated during its fall.
E) Will have the same acceleration during each second of its fall.

questions.explanation: In free fall (vacuum, no air resistance), the acceleration is constant (g = 9.8 m/s²) throughout the fall, regardless of speed.

questions.question: Q7. A bowling ball at a height of 36 meters above the ground is falling vertically at a rate of 12 meters per second. Which of these best describes its fate?

options.text: A) It will hit the ground in exactly 3 seconds at a speed of 12 m/s
B) It will hit the ground in less than 3 seconds at a speed greater than 12 m/s
C) It will hit the ground in more than 3 seconds at a speed less than 12 m/s
D) It will hit the ground in less than 3 seconds at a speed less than 12 m/s
E) It will hit the ground in more than 3 seconds at a speed greater than 12 m/s

questions.question: Q8. The speedometer in your car tells you the _________ of your car.
questions.explanation: A speedometer shows the speed at that instant in time, i.e. instantaneous speed, not average speed.

questions.question: Q9. To report the _________ of an object, we must specify both its speed and its direction.
questions.explanation: Velocity is a vector — it requires both magnitude (speed) and direction to be fully described.

questions.question: Q10. Projectile 'A' is fired at an angle of 50° above the horizontal; projectile 'B' is fired with the same speed at an angle of 40° above the horizontal. Assuming level ground and negligible air resistance, which of the following is true?

options.text: A) 'A' will reach a greater height and have a greater range than 'B'.
B) 'A' will reach a greater height and have the same range as 'B'.
C) 'A' will reach a greater height and have a shorter range than 'B'.
D) 'A' will reach the same height and have the same range as 'B'.
E) 'A' will reach the same height and have a shorter range than 'B'.

questions.explanation: Complementary angles (50° and 40°, summing to 90°) give the same range. The higher launch angle (50°, closer to 90°) reaches a greater maximum height.

questions.question: Q11. In absence of air resistance, the magnitude of the vertical component of a projectile's acceleration

options.text: A) is constant until the projectile hits the ground.
B) always decreases with time until the projectile hits the ground.
C) is equal to the magnitude of the horizontal component of the projectile's acceleration.
D) increases and or decreases with time, depending on the projectile's velocity.
E) always increases with time until the projectile hits the ground.

questions.explanation: With no air resistance, gravity is the only vertical force, so vertical acceleration (and hence the rate the vertical component changes) stays constant until landing.

questions.question: Q12. A ball is thrown horizontally with a speed of 25 m/s from the top of a tower 20 meters high. Assuming level ground below the negligible air resistance, what will be the magnitude of the vertical velocity component when ball hits the ground?
questions.explanation: Horizontal velocity is unaffected by gravity in projectile motion (no horizontal force acts), so it stays at 25 m/s... (note: check option wording against 20 m/s if height changes horizontal component — here horizontal speed remains constant throughout the flight).

questions.question: Q13. Which of these is the best description of the trajectory of a projectile short from the top of a high cliff at an angle of 60° below the horizontal (neglecting air resistance)?

options.text: A) The projectile will moves downwards at a 60° angle in a straight line at a constant speed until it stops and then falls straight down.
B) The projectile will moves downwards at a 60° angle in a straight line at a gradually diminishing speed until it stops and then falls straight down.
C) The projectile will moves downwards at a 60° angle in a straight line at a gradually increasing speed until it stops and then falls straight down.
D) The projectile will gradually are downward, following the curve of a circle.
E) The projectile will gradually are downward, following the curve of a parabola.

questions.explanation: With gravity constantly pulling it down while it moves forward, a projectile follows a smooth curved (parabolic) path, not a straight line that suddenly drops.

questions.question: Q14. A firefighter with a mass of 70 kg slides down a vertical pole, accelerating at 2 m/s². The forces of friction that acts on the firefighter is
questions.explanation: Net force = ma, so friction (normal force from pole) = mg − ma = 70(9.8 − 2) ≈ 560 N, opposing gravity to produce the given acceleration.

questions.question: Q15. The _________ of an object on the Earth's surface are directly proportional each other.
questions.explanation: Weight = mass × g, so on Earth's surface (where g is constant) mass and weight are directly proportional to each other.

questions.question: Q16. The Moon's gravity is 1/6 of the Earth's gravity. The weight of a bowling ball on the Earth would be _________ its weight on the Moon.
questions.explanation: Since Moon gravity is 1/6 of Earth's, the same object weighs 1/6 as much on the Moon — equivalently, it weighs 6× more on Earth than on the Moon.

questions.question: Q17. When a certain net force is applied to one brick on a frictionless surface, it accelerates at 6 m/s². When the same net force is applied three bricks that are cemented together.

options.text: E) they do not accelerate at all

questions.explanation: Same force divides equally between identical bricks in a train being pushed together — same net force, same total mass ratio, so acceleration is unchanged for both.

questions.question: Q18. To accelerate a 6 kg mass at 2 m/s² requires a net force of _________.
questions.explanation: F = ma = 6 kg × 2 m/s² = 12 N.

questions.question: Q19. A falling object is said to reach terminal speed

options.text: A) when it lands on the ground
B) when its air resistance equals the force of gravity on it.
C) when there is no air resistance acting on it.
D) when there is no gravitational force acting on it.

questions.explanation: Terminal velocity is reached when the upward air resistance force exactly balances the downward force of gravity, giving zero net force and constant speed.

questions.question: Q20. For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. This is a statement of

options.text: A) Newton's First Law of Motion.
B) Newton's Second Law of Motion.
C) Newton's Third Law of Motion.
D) Newton's Fourth Law of Motion.

questions.explanation: This is the exact statement of Newton's Third Law of Motion: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

questions.question: Q21. An airplane flying east at an airspeed of 200 km/h has a headwind blowing from the east at 50 km/h. How far will the plane fly relative to the ground in two hours?
questions.explanation: Headwind subtracts from airspeed relative to ground; over time this changes distance/ground speed — with the given numbers, ground speed calculation yields 300 km (context-dependent on time given in original problem).

questions.question: Q22. An airplane heading west at an airspeed of 100 km/h has a crosswind blowing from the south at 100 km/h. What will be the airplane's speed relative to the ground?
questions.explanation: Airspeed and crosswind are perpendicular, so ground speed = √(100² + 100²) ≈ 141 km/h (vector sum of perpendicular components).

questions.question: Q23. _________ are examples of vector quantities.
questions.explanation: Velocity and acceleration both have direction as well as magnitude, making them vector quantities (unlike speed or distance, which are scalars).

questions.question: Q24. A green ball moving to the right at 3 m/s strikes a yellow ball moving to the left at 2 m/s. If the balls are equally massive and the collision is elastic.

options.text: A) The green ball will move to the left at 3 m/s while the yellow ball moves right at 2 m/s.
B) The green ball will move to the left at 2 m/s while the yellow ball moves right at 3 m/s.
C) The green ball will stop while the yellow ball moves right at 2 m/s.
D) The yellow ball will stop while the green ball moves left at 3 m/s.
E) Both balls will stick together and move to the right at 1 m/s.

questions.explanation: In an elastic, equal-and-opposite momentum exchange between identical balls, the two simply swap velocities: the green ball takes on the yellow ball's leftward 2 m/s, and vice versa.

questions.question: Q25. An impulse of 100 N-s is applied to an object. If this same impulse is delivered over a longer time interval.

options.text: A) the force involved will be decreased.
B) the force involved will be increased.
C) the momentum transferred will be increased.
D) the momentum transferred will be decreased.
E) the acceleration involved will be increased.

questions.explanation: Impulse = F × t is fixed at 100 N·s. If the time over which it's applied increases, the force must decrease to keep the impulse the same.

questions.question: Q26. Case 1: A net force of 10 N acts on a mass of 1 kg for a time of 0.2 s. Case 2: A net force of 20 N acts on a mass of 1 kg for a time of 0.2 s.

options.text: A) involve the same impulse and produce the same acceleration.
B) involve the same impulse and produce the different accelerations.
C) involve different impulses and produce different accelerations.
D) involve different impulses and produce the same acceleration.
E) produce the same change of momentum.

questions.explanation: Impulse = F×t is different in each case (different F and/or t), and since impulse = change in momentum, differing impulses produce differing accelerations/velocity changes.

questions.question: Q27. Momentum is the product of
questions.explanation: Momentum is defined as p = m × v, the product of an object's mass and its velocity.

questions.question: Q28. If a moving object cuts its speed in half, how much momentum will it have?

options.text: A) the same amount as before
B) twice as much as before.
C) one half as much as before.
D) four times as much as before
E) one fourth as much as before

questions.explanation: Momentum is proportional to velocity (p = mv). Halving speed while mass stays the same halves the momentum.

questions.question: Q29. A 1 kg ball moving horizontally to the right at 3 m/s strikes a wall and rebounds, moving horizontally to the left at the same speed. What is the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball?
questions.explanation: The ball's momentum changes from +3 kg·m/s to −3 kg·m/s (rebounds), so the change in momentum has magnitude |−3 − 3| = 6 kg·m/s (impulse delivered by the wall).

questions.question: Q30. Potential energy is the energy possessed by an object due to
questions.explanation: Potential energy is stored energy that depends on an object's position (e.g. height in a gravitational field) or configuration.

questions.question: Q31. Which of the following is true?

options.text: A) A body with zero velocity cannot have any potential energy.
B) A body with zero acceleration cannot have any kinetic energy.
C) A body with zero acceleration cannot have any potential energy.
D) A body with zero velocity cannot have any kinetic energy.
E) A body with zero potential energy cannot have velocity

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy = ½mv². If velocity is zero, KE = 0 regardless of mass, so a body at rest cannot have kinetic energy.

questions.question: Q32. If two objects of different mass have the same non-zero momentum.

options.text: A) the one with less mass will have the greater kinetic energy.
B) the one with more mass will have the greater kinetic energy.
C) they will have the same kinetic energy.
D) the one with the higher speed will have the greater mass.
E) the one with the lower speed will have the greater kinetic energy.

questions.explanation: KE = p²/2m for fixed momentum p. Since KE is inversely proportional to mass here, the lighter object has more kinetic energy.

questions.question: Q33. A car travelling at 60 km/h passes a truck going 30 km/h that has four times the mass of the car. Which of the following is time?

options.text: A) the car and the truck have the same momentum and the same kinetic energy.
B) the car has the same momentum and twice as much kinetic energy as the truck.
C) the car has the same momentum and four times as much kinetic energy as the truck.
D) the car has the same kinetic energy and twice as much momentum as the truck.
E) the car has the same kinetic energy and half as much momentum as the truck.

questions.explanation: KE = ½mv², and with car speed double the truck's, (½)(m)(2v)² = 2mv², while the truck has mass 4m at speed v giving ½(4m)(v²)=2mv² — equal KE. Momentum p=mv: car has mv(2)=2mv, truck has 4m(v)=4mv, so car has half the truck's momentum.

questions.question: Q34. A swinging pendulum has __________ at the bottom (middle) of its are
questions.explanation: At the bottom of its swing the pendulum is at its lowest height, so gravitational potential energy (which depends on height) is at its minimum there.

questions.question: Q35. Real machines are not 100% efficient because

options.text: A) some of the energy input is always transformed into thermal energy.
B) some of the input is always transformed into gravitational potential energy.
C) the energy input is always less than the energy output.
D) that would require the work output to be 100 times the work input, which is impossible.
E) that would require the work input to be 100 times the work output, which is impossible.

questions.explanation: No real machine is 100% efficient because friction and other resistive forces always convert some input energy into heat (thermal energy), which is 'lost' as useful output.

questions.question: Q36. A physicist does 100 joules of work on a sample machine that raises a box of books through a high of 0.2 meters. If the efficiency of the machine is 60%, how much work is converted to thermal energy by this process?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = useful output / input. With losses, only a fraction of the 100 J input goes into raising the box; the given options make 40 J the efficient/useful output here.

questions.question: Q37. When you run up two flights of stairs instead of walking up them, you feel more tired because

options.text: A) you do more work when you run than when you walk.
B) your power output is greater when you run than when you walk.
C) the gravitational is greater on a running person then on a walking person.
D) the gravitational acceleration is greater on a running person then on a walking person.
E) a running person has more inertia than a walking person.

questions.explanation: Power = work/time. Running up the stairs does the same total work as walking but in less time, so your power output (rate of doing work) is higher — hence more tiredness.

questions.question: Q38. The work done against gravity in moving a box with a mass of 5 kilograms through a height of 3 meters is
questions.explanation: W = mgh = 5 kg × 9.8 m/s² × height. Given the answer of 150 J with these numbers implies a height of about 3 m used in the original problem.

questions.question: Q39. Angular momentum is the product of

options.text: A) rotational inertia and rotational velocity.

questions.explanation: Angular momentum L = I × ω, the product of rotational inertia (I) and rotational (angular) velocity (ω) — the rotational analog of linear momentum.

questions.question: Q40. When you stand in equilibrium on only 1 foot,

options.text: A) your center of mass will be directly above that foot
B) your center of mass will be directly other foot
C) your center of mass will be directly above a point equidistant between your two feet.
D) your rotational inertia will be zero
E) you will always fall over

questions.explanation: For stable equilibrium while balancing on one foot, your center of mass must be directly above your base of support (that foot) so there's no net torque.

questions.question: Q41. When a car rounds a curve at high speed,

options.text: A) the tires exert a centripetal force on the road.
B) the road exerts a centripetal force on the tires
C) the car exerts a centripetal force on the road
D) the car body exerts a centripetal force on the tires
E) there are no centripetal force involved

questions.explanation: When a car turns, friction between tires and road supplies the centripetal force needed to keep the car moving along the curved path.

questions.question: Q42. On a spinning disk point closers to the outer edge will have _______ point near the center.

options.text: A) the same rotational speed as and greater tangential speed than
B) the same rotational speed as and lower tangential speed than
C) the same tangential speed as and greater rotational speed than
D) the same tangential speed as and lower rotational speed than
E) lower rotational speed and higher tangential speed than

questions.explanation: All points on a rigid rotating disk share the same rotational (angular) speed, but points farther from the center move faster in a straight-line (tangential) sense since they cover more distance per rotation.

questions.question: Q43. A merry-go round rotates 9 times each minute such that a point on its rim moves at a rate of 3 m/s. At a point 2/3 of the way out from the center to the rim, the tangential speed would be ______
questions.explanation: Tangential speed v = ωr is proportional to radius r for fixed angular speed ω. At 2/3 of the radius, v = (2/3)(3 m/s) = 2 m/s.

questions.question: Q44. An empty soup can and a full one are rolled side-by-side down an incline. If they start together, which one will reach the bottom first?

options.text: A) the empty can arrives first
B) the fall can arrives first.
D) it depends on the diameter of the cans
E) it depends on the kind of soup

questions.explanation: A solid, full can has different mass distribution (more concentrated near the axis, effectively lower rotational inertia relative to mass) allowing it to convert more potential energy into linear motion (translational KE) and roll down faster than a partially hollow or differently distributed can.

questions.question: Q45. A mass of 1 kilogram is tied to a string and swing in a horizontal circle of radius 1 meter, if the mass is then decreased to 0.5 kilogram, the potential inertia of this new system will be ______ as before.
questions.explanation: Doubling radius while keeping angular speed and speed constraints from a circular motion problem — for the given setup, tension/force scales such that it works out to half the original value.

questions.question: Q46. Torque is the product of

options.text: E) lever arm and rotational inertia

questions.explanation: Torque = force × lever arm (perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force).

questions.question: Q47. A 60-kg grandfather and his 30-kg granddaughter are balanced on a seesaw. If the granddaughter is sitting 2 meters from the pivot point, the grandfather must be sitting _______ from it
questions.explanation: For balance (equal torques): 60 kg × d1 = 30 kg × d2. If the grandfather sits 1 m from the pivot, the granddaughter must sit 2 m out — matching option consistent with a 1 m distance for the heavier person.

questions.question: Q48. Protons have _____ charge, neutrons have _____ charge, and electrons have _____ charge.
questions.explanation: Protons carry positive charge, neutrons are electrically neutral (no charge), and electrons carry negative charge — the basic composition of an atom.

questions.question: Q49. Which of the following is true?

options.text: A) some atoms do not belong to any particular element
B) some atoms belong to more than one element
D) the number of protons in an atom determines which elements it is
E) the number of neutrons in an atom determines which elements it is

questions.explanation: The number of protons (atomic number) uniquely defines which element an atom is; the number of neutrons or electrons can vary (isotopes, ions) without changing the element.

questions.question: Q50. The mass of 1 hydrogen atom is approximately
questions.explanation: A single hydrogen atom (1 proton, 1 electron, essentially no neutron in the common isotope) has a mass of approximately 1 atomic mass unit (u), which is how the amu scale is defined.

questions.question: Q51. An element with an atomic number of 92 at an atomic mass number of 238 would have
questions.explanation: Atomic number 92 = 92 protons = 92 electrons (neutral atom). Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 238 − 92 = 146.

questions.question: Q52. Brownian motion is the

options.text: A) random motion of microscopic particles being bombarded by even smaller atoms and molecules
B) random motion of atoms and molecules being bombarded by larger microscopic particles
C) vibration of atoms and molecules in a solid
D) movement of electrons circulating within the atom
E) very gradual flow of solid materials such as glass over long periods of time.

questions.explanation: Brownian motion is the observed random, jittery motion of small (but visible) particles caused by countless collisions with much smaller, fast-moving molecules of the surrounding fluid.

questions.question: Q53. Chemical combinations of elements are called
questions.explanation: When two or more elements chemically combine in fixed proportions, the resulting substances are called compounds.

questions.question: Q54. Which of the following is a list of elements?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen are each pure substances made of only one type of atom, making them elements (not compounds or mixtures).

questions.question: Q55. Where on the periodic table would we find an element with one more proton and one more electron than silver?

options.text: B) just to the left of silver.
D) just to the right of silver.
E) None of these – there is no such element.

questions.explanation: Adding one proton and one neutron moves you one position to the right along the same period on the periodic table (next element by atomic number).

questions.question: Q56. Density is
questions.explanation: Density is defined as an object's mass divided by its volume (ρ = m/V).

questions.question: Q57. 1000 cubic centimeters of water should have a mass of approximately ________.
questions.explanation: Water has a density of about 1 g/cm³, so 1000 cm³ has a mass of about 1000 g = 1 kg.

questions.question: Q58. A material is said to be _______ if it changes shape when a deforming force acts on it and returns to its original shape when the deforming force is removed.
questions.explanation: A material that permanently changes shape under a deforming force (rather than returning to its original shape) is described in this context by the given option — though note 'elastic' materials actually return to shape; check this option against the exact phrasing used.

questions.question: Q59. Hooke's law relates the

options.text: A) distance a spring stretches to the force applied to the spring.
B) distance a spring stretches to the mass applied to the spring.
C) distance a spring stretches to the density applied to the spring.
D) density of a spring to the force applied to the spring.
E) density of a spring to the mass of the spring.

questions.explanation: Hooke's Law states that the extension (stretch) of a spring is directly proportional to the applied force, within the elastic limit.

questions.question: Q60. When the length of each edge of a cube is doubled, the cube's surface area increases by a factor of
questions.explanation: Surface area of a cube scales with the square of its edge length. Doubling the edge multiplies surface area by 2² = 4.

questions.question: Q61. When the length of each edge of a cube is tripled, the cube's volume

options.text: A) increases by a factor of 3.
B) decreases by a factor of 1/3.
C) increases by a factor of 9.
D) decreases by a factor of 1/9.
E) increases by a factor of 27.

questions.explanation: Volume of a cube scales with the cube of its edge length. Tripling the edge multiplies volume by 3³ = 27.

questions.question: Q62. Maximum number of beats per sound second is _____ which can be heard by human ear.
questions.explanation: The human ear can distinguish/count individual beats up to about 7 beats per second before they blend into a continuous tone (a standard textbook figure).

questions.question: Q63. Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a medium is called.
questions.explanation: Refractive index n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the given medium.

questions.question: Q64. In Galleon telescope, the final image formed is.
questions.explanation: In a Galilean telescope (convex objective + concave eyepiece), the final image produced is virtual and erect (upright), unlike the astronomical (Keplerian) telescope which gives an inverted image.

questions.question: Q65. An object with a mass of 1 kg displaces 700 ml of water. Which of the following is true?

options.text: A) the weight of this object is 10 N.
B) the weight of this object is 7 N.
C) the weight of this object is 3 N.
D) the buoyant force on this object is 3 N.
E) the buoyant force on this object is 10 N.

questions.explanation: Weight = mg = 1 kg × ~9.8–10 m/s² ≈ 10 N, independent of how much water it displaces (that relates to buoyancy, not weight).

questions.question: Q66. An object with a mass of 1 kg displaces 0.6 kg of water. Which of the following is true?

options.text: A) the buoyant force on this object is 10 N.
B) the buoyant force on this object is 6 N.
C) the buoyant force on this object is 4 N.
D) the density of this object is less than that of water.
E) this object will not sink in water.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced: 0.6 kg of water displaced → weight = 0.6 × 10 ≈ 6 N of buoyant force (Archimedes' Principle).

questions.question: Q67. The water pressure in a lake behind a dam depends on

options.text: A) the volume of lake water behind the dam.
B) the surface area of the lake.
C) the distance from the dam at which the pressure is measured.
D) the depth below the surface at which the pressure is measured.
E) the number of fish in the lake.

questions.explanation: Fluid pressure in a lake increases with depth (P = ρgh); it does not depend on the total volume or surface area of the lake, only the depth at the measurement point.

questions.question: Q68. When air is removed from a metal can by a vacuum pump, the can buckles inwards and is crushed. This occurs because

options.text: A) the air pressure on the inside of the can is greater than the air pressure on the outside of the can.
B) the air pressure on the outside of the can is greater than the air pressure on the inside of the can.
C) the loss of air molecules from inside the can weakens the metal.
D) the opposite sides of the empty can strongly attract each other.

questions.explanation: Removing air lowers the internal pressure. Since outside atmospheric pressure now exceeds the (near-vacuum) internal pressure, the net inward force crushes the can.

questions.question: Q69. Bernoulli's Principle explants why

options.text: A) a hot air balloon rises.
B) liquid rises in a drinking straw.

questions.explanation: Bernoulli's Principle explains that faster-moving air over a curved wing surface has lower pressure than the slower air beneath, creating lift — this is why airplanes fly.

questions.question: Q70. In order to decrease the pressure in an automobile tire, one normally

options.text: A) decreases the temperature of the tire.
B) increases the volume of the tire.
C) increases the density of air in the tire.
D) decreases the surface area of the tire.

questions.explanation: This option's phrasing is unusual (decreasing pressure by decreasing surface area doesn't match physics); typically you decrease tire pressure by releasing air. Flag this option for review against the intended physics.

questions.question: Q71. According to Boyle's Law, if the volume occupied by a certain gas is doubled,

options.text: A) the pressure of the gas will be doubled.
B) the pressure of the gas will be quadrupled.
C) the pressure of the gas will remain constant.
D) the pressure of the gas will be halved.
E) the number of atoms in the gas will be halved.

questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related (PV = constant). Doubling volume halves the pressure.

questions.question: Q72. Archimedes' Principle states that an object surrounded by air is buoyed up by a force equal to the

options.text: A) weight of the air displaces.
C) total pressure on the object.
D) difference between the weight of the object and the weight of the air it displaces.

questions.explanation: Archimedes' Principle: any object surrounded by a fluid (including air) experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

questions.question: Q73. In general, when a liquid is heated

options.text: A) it will neither expand nor contract.
B) it will expend at a greater rate than a solid.
C) it will expend at a lesser rate than a solid.
D) it will contract at a greater rate than a solid.
E) it will contract at a lesser rate than a solid.

questions.explanation: Liquids generally have higher thermal expansion coefficients than solids, so a heated liquid expands faster/more than an equivalently heated solid.

questions.question: Q74. It a heat metal plate with a circular hole cut through it is heated,

options.text: C) the hole stays exactly the same size.
D) the hole may get larger or smaller, depending on the material of the plate.
E) the hole may get larger or smaller, depending on how much the plate is heated.

questions.explanation: When a metal plate with a hole is heated, the whole plate (including the hole) expands proportionally, so the hole gets larger, not smaller — this is thermal expansion.

questions.question: Q75. Water has a higher specific heat capacity than iron. This means that

options.text: A) water is more dense than iron.
B) water is hotter than higher.
C) water heats more rapidly than iron.
D) water heats more slowly than iron.
E) water boils at a higher temperature than iron.

questions.explanation: Higher specific heat means more energy is needed to raise the temperature by the same amount, so for the same heat input, water's temperature rises more slowly than iron's.

questions.question: Q76. The specific heat capacity of water is 1 calorie per gram per degree Celsius. This means that it will take _______ calorie(s) to increases the temperature of 10 grams of water by 10 degrees.
questions.explanation: Heat required Q = mcΔT = (10 g)(1 cal/g°C)(10°C) = 100 calories.

questions.question: Q77. Water reaches its highest density at a temperature of ______ degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: Water is unusual in that its density peaks at 4°C (not at 0°C), due to hydrogen-bonding effects, before it starts expanding again as it approaches freezing.

questions.question: Q78. Which of these is an example of heat transfer by conduction?

options.text: A) The handle of a metal spoon becomes hot when you use it to stir a pot of soup on the stove.
B) The air near the ceiling is normally warmer than air near the floor.
C) You can boil a water in microwave oven.
D) You feel heat from a bonfire even though you are several meters away from it.
E) Smoke rises up a chimney.

questions.explanation: Conduction is heat transfer through direct contact within a material — heat travels up the solid metal spoon into your hand, a classic conduction example.

questions.question: Q79. Rising air tends to.

options.text: E) Maintain a constant density and temperature.

questions.explanation: As air rises, it moves into regions of lower atmospheric pressure, so it expands; this expansion does work on its surroundings and causes it to cool (adiabatic cooling).

questions.question: Q80. Radiation is heat transfer by.
questions.explanation: Radiation transfers heat via electromagnetic waves (like infrared), and unlike conduction/convection, requires no medium — it can travel through a vacuum.

questions.question: Q81. The pattern formed by overlapping waves in a bow wave is in the shape of the letter ____.
questions.explanation: The V-shaped wake pattern seen behind a boat (a bow wave) is formed by overlapping circular waves interfering constructively along diagonal lines.

questions.question: Q82. The Doppler Effect causes.

options.text: A) The observed pitch of a sound to be lower if the source of sound is approaching the observer.
B) The observed pitch of a sound to be higher if the source of sound is moving away from the observer.
C) The observed pitch of a sound to be lower if the source of sound is moving away from the observer.
D) The speed of sound to increases if the source of sound is moving away from the observer.
E) The speed of sound to decrease if the source of sound is moving away from the observer.

questions.explanation: The Doppler Effect causes a lower observed pitch (frequency) when the sound source moves away from the observer, since sound waves get 'stretched out.'

questions.question: Q83. In a ______ wave, the medium vibrates in a direction that is perpendicular to the direction the wave travels.
questions.explanation: In a transverse wave, particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels (e.g. water waves, light waves).

questions.question: Q84. The period of a pendulum depend on.

options.text: A) The mass of the pendulum and the size of the are it swings through.
B) The length of the pendulum and the size of the are it swings through.
C) The mass of the pendulum and the acceleration of gravity.
D) The length of the pendulum and the acceleration of gravity.
E) The weight of pendulum and the material it is made from.

questions.explanation: For a simple pendulum, T = 2π√(L/g) — the period depends only on its length and the local acceleration due to gravity (not mass or amplitude, for small swings).

questions.question: Q85. A wave that has a relatively long wavelength will also have a relatively.
questions.explanation: Wave speed v = fλ. For waves of similar speed, a longer wavelength corresponds to a lower frequency, and since period T = 1/f, a lower frequency means a longer period.

questions.question: Q86. A train of freight cars, each 10m long, rolls by the rates of 2 cars each sound. What is the speed of train?
questions.explanation: Speed = (cars per second) × (length per car) = 2 cars/s × 10 m = 20 m/s.

questions.question: Q87. Compared a 500-Hz sound, a 300-Hz sound would have.

options.text: A) A longer wavelength and the same speed.
B) A longer wavelength and the lower speed.
C) A longer wavelength and the higher speed.
D) A shorter wavelength and the lower speed.
E) A shorter wavelength and the same speed.

questions.explanation: Lower frequency corresponds to a longer wavelength (v = fλ, same speed medium), so a 300 Hz tone has a longer wavelength than 500 Hz at the same sound speed.

questions.question: Q88. A vibrating string is being tuned to match a timing fork with a frequency of 256 Hz. When 3 beats per sound and heard, the vibration frequency of the string must be.
questions.explanation: Beat frequency = |f_string − f_fork|. With 3 beats/s and fork at 256 Hz, the string could be at either 256−3=253 Hz or 256+3=259 Hz — beats alone can't tell you which side.

questions.question: Q89. Constructive interference of sound wave occur.

options.text: A) Whenever there is an echo.
B) When two waves arrive at the same point in phase with each other.
C) When two waves arrive at the same point out phase with each other.
D) Whenever sound waves are refracted by air layers of different temperatures.
E) Whenever sound waves are refracted off distant building.

questions.explanation: Constructive interference happens when two waves meet in phase (crest aligns with crest), reinforcing each other to produce a larger amplitude.

questions.question: Q90. Pushing a person on a swing at the same rate as the natural frequency of the swing/pendulum is an example of.
questions.explanation: Driving a system at its natural frequency causes amplitude to build up dramatically — this phenomenon is called resonance.

questions.question: Q91. Sound travels faster in air at.

options.text: A) Lower temperatures because the molecules move faster and collide more frequently.
B) Lower temperatures because the molecules are closer together and colli more frequently.
C) Higher temperatures because the molecules move faster and collide more frequently.
D) Higher temperatures because the molecules are closer together and collide more frequently.
E) Lower temperatures because the air is more solid then.

questions.explanation: Sound travels through a medium via molecular collisions; at higher temperatures molecules move faster and collide more often, transmitting the wave more quickly.

questions.question: Q92. An intensity of 60 decibels is ____ times as intense as an intensity of 30 decibels.
questions.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic: a 30 dB increase corresponds to a factor of 10^(30/10) = 10³ = 1000 times greater intensity.

questions.question: Q93. The "Highness" or "lowness" of a musical tune is called ________.
questions.explanation: The perceived highness or lowness of a musical note (related to frequency) is called its pitch.

questions.question: Q94. Partial tones whose frequencies are whole number multiples of the fundamental frequency are called
questions.explanation: Overtones whose frequencies are exact whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency are called harmonics.

questions.question: Q95. When a guitar string vibrates at the frequency of it's third harmonic, it will have a node at each end and _______ in between.
questions.explanation: The third harmonic has 3 antinode segments (loops) and therefore 4 total nodes: one at each fixed end plus two additional nodes in between.

questions.question: Q96. A capacitor is a device used to

options.text: C) Force current through a wire
E) measure the volume of a glass container

questions.explanation: A capacitor stores electrical energy by holding separated positive and negative charges on its two plates.

questions.question: Q97. A positively charged object.

options.text: A) has a deficiency of protons
B) has a deficiency of neutrons
C) has a deficiency of electrons
D) has an excess of electrons
E) has an excess of neutrons

questions.explanation: An object becomes positively charged when it loses electrons, i.e. has a deficiency (shortage) of electrons relative to protons.

questions.question: Q98. Good electrical insulators are usually.
questions.explanation: Field lines from an isolated point charge radiate outward (or inward) symmetrically in all directions, forming concentric spherical patterns (circles in a 2D cross-section) around it.

questions.question: Q99. The lines of force for a point charge

options.text: A) Form concentric circles about it
B) extend radially outward from it
C) connect points of equal electric potential
D) connect points of equal charge
E) Indicate the direction of motion of the point charge

questions.explanation: Good electrical insulators, by their nature of tightly bound electrons, also tend to conduct heat poorly, not well — this option should be checked against the intended physics if marked otherwise.

questions.question: Q100. According to Coulomb's Law, if the distance between two charges is doubled, the force each charge exerts on the other will be _______ it's previous value
questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law: F ∝ 1/r². Doubling the distance r reduces the force to 1/2² = 1/4 of its original value.

questions.question: Q101. The intensity level of sound if intensity 10(-12) watt/m² in a bell is
questions.explanation: Sound intensity level β = log₁₀(I/I₀), where I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² is the reference (threshold of hearing) intensity. When I equals I₀, log₁₀(1) = 0, so the level is zero.

questions.question: Q102. A body of mass 10 kg start falling freely. The height lost in the 1st second is.
questions.explanation: Distance fallen in time t from rest: h = ½gt². For t = 1 s, h = ½(9.8)(1)² = 4.9 m.

questions.question: Q103. The units of angular momentum are.
questions.explanation: Angular momentum L = Iω has units of kg·m²/s, which is dimensionally the same as Joule-seconds (since 1 J = 1 kg·m²/s², so 1 J·s = 1 kg·m²/s).

questions.question: Q104. Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: A scalar quantity has magnitude only, no direction. Speed is scalar, while velocity, acceleration, and displacement are all vectors.

questions.question: Q105. One radian is equal to.
questions.explanation: One radian is the angle subtended when arc length equals the radius; converting to degrees, 1 rad = 180°/π ≈ 57.3°.

questions.question: Q106. If two forces of the same magnitude F are acting at an angle 120° with each other, the magnitude of their resultant will be.
questions.explanation: Resultant of two equal forces F at 120° apart: R = √(F² + F² + 2F²cos120°) = √(2F² − F²) = F.

questions.question: Q107. A wave enters from one medium to another medium, no change occurs in its.
questions.explanation: When a wave crosses into a new medium, its frequency stays the same (set by the source), while its speed and wavelength change.

questions.question: Q108. The velocity of a body after elastic collision with a body of the same mass at rest will be.
questions.explanation: In an elastic collision between equal masses where one is initially at rest, the moving object transfers all its momentum and kinetic energy to the stationary one, coming to a complete stop (velocity becomes zero).

questions.question: Q109. If a man go to a height, double to the radius of the earth from its surface, his weight relative to the weight on earth's surface will be.
questions.explanation: Gravitational field strength g ∝ 1/r² from Earth's center. At a height equal to Earth's radius, total distance from center = 2R, so g becomes (1/2)² = 1/4 of its surface value, and weight becomes one-fourth.

questions.question: Q110. When a dielectric is placed in an electric field, it becomes?
questions.explanation: An electric field causes the positive and negative charges within a dielectric material to shift slightly apart, aligning them — this is called polarization.

questions.question: Q111. The internal energy in an isothermal process.
questions.explanation: In an isothermal process, temperature is constant, and for an ideal gas internal energy depends only on temperature, so internal energy remains unchanged (ΔU = 0) — all heat input goes into work done.

questions.question: Q112. The frequencies in spectral lines emitted in Lyman series are in the region of.
questions.explanation: The Lyman series (electron transitions to the n=1 level in hydrogen) produces the highest-energy, shortest-wavelength lines, which fall in the ultraviolet region of the spectrum.

questions.question: Q113. The distance between node and anti-node in a loop is.
questions.explanation: In a standing wave, adjacent nodes and antinodes are separated by a quarter wavelength (λ/4); a full loop (node to node) spans λ/2.

questions.question: Q114. A force F = 4i − 2j is applied in moving an object along a displacement r = 3i + 4j.
Q115. The energy required to overcome the binding force is called.
questions.explanation: The minimum energy needed to free an electron from a material's surface (overcoming the attractive binding force) is called the work function.

questions.question: Q116. The magnetic field of induction 'B' inside the solenoid is.
questions.explanation: Inside a long solenoid, the magnetic field is strong and essentially uniform along its length — comparatively it is at its maximum value there versus outside the solenoid, where it rapidly weakens.

questions.question: Q117. When a body moves vertically upward, the work done by gravitational force will be.
questions.explanation: As a body moves upward, gravity (pointing downward) opposes the displacement, so the work done by gravity is negative (force and displacement are in opposite directions).

questions.question: Q118. The structure of a crystal can be studied with the help of.
questions.explanation: X-ray diffraction through the regularly spaced atomic planes of a crystal produces interference patterns that reveal the crystal's internal structure (crystallography).

questions.question: Q119. The unit of power of a lens is.
questions.explanation: The power of a lens (P = 1/f, with f in meters) is measured in diopters.

questions.question: Q120. If the tension of stretched string is increased 4 times, the speed of the transverse wave in it will increase.
questions.explanation: Transverse wave speed on a string: v = √(T/μ). If tension T increases 4×, speed increases by √4 = 2×.
